heading: The December bonus test
lede: Seven quick winter questions, just for people on my list. Grab a brew.
intro: Frost, snow, sprouts and a bit of Christmas. Seven questions, about two minutes. Can you get all seven?
june: Thanks for playing. There's a new one in my email at the start of every month, so keep an eye out in January.

levels.name: Frosty start
levels.line: A chilly start, but now you know. Winter's the best time to learn.

levels.name: Thawing out
levels.line: Not bad at all. A couple of these catch everyone out.

levels.name: Winter ready
levels.line: Proper winter gardener. Your plot's in good hands.

levels.name: Christmas cracker
levels.line: Seven out of seven. You can carve the parsnips this year.

questions.q: Parsnips taste sweeter after a hard frost.
questions.alt: A muddy parsnip pulled from a frosty raised bed
questions.why: Fact. A good frost brings out their sweetness and flavour.
questions.tip: Parsnips are tough enough to stay in the ground all winter, so dig them as you need them. Lift a few before a big freeze, or lay straw over the row, because frozen ground is a pig to dig.

questions.q: Odd one out on a UK plot in December?
questions.why: Courgettes. The first frost finishes them off, while the other three sit happily through winter.
questions.tip: Sprouts, leeks and well covered carrots can all be picked through the cold months. Courgettes are a summer crop: sow them indoors in spring and plant out once the frosts are over.

questions.q: Which of these is the same plant species as a Brussels sprout?
questions.why: Kale. Sprouts, kale, cabbage and broccoli are all Brassica oleracea.
questions.tip: Because they're one family, grow them in the same bed in your rotation and net them all against pigeons and cabbage white butterflies. Garlic and onions go together in another bed, and beans in another.

questions.q: Bare root fruit bushes like this. When do they go in?
questions.alt: A gloved hand holding a bare root fruit bush by a fence, ready to plant

options.label: In spring, once they're in leaf
Midsummer, when the soil is warm

questions.why: Now. Bare root fruit is planted while dormant, November to March.
questions.tip: Plant them straight away when they arrive, on any day the ground isn't frozen or waterlogged. If it is, stand the roots in a bucket of damp compost for a few days until it eases.

questions.q: Why do gardeners put a bucket over a rhubarb crown in winter?
questions.alt: A rhubarb crown with pink buds in bare winter soil

options.label: To keep the frost off it
To force early, tender pink stems

questions.why: In the dark the stems grow faster, paler, sweeter and more tender.
questions.tip: Cover a healthy crown that's been in at least three years in January, with a forcing pot or a tall bucket so the stems have 30cm to grow. Pick in about eight weeks, then give that crown a few years off.

questions.q: Heavy snow is weighing down your hedge and shrubs. What do you do?

options.label: Leave it, snow keeps them warm
Gently shake it off the branches

questions.why: Shake the weight off so the branches don't bend and snap.
questions.tip: Use a broom or a gentle shake, working upwards from the bottom. If heavy snow is forecast, move pots of tender plants somewhere sheltered first, such as a greenhouse or porch.

questions.q: Every holly bush will give you red berries for Christmas.
questions.why: Myth. Only female hollies berry, and most need a male nearby.
questions.tip: Check the label before you buy. The names can fool you: 'Golden King' is a female and 'Silver Queen' is a male. 'J.C. van Tol' is one that berries on its own.
